newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Tension, but no bloodshed at Islamic shrine.
newsitem.headline: Tension, but no bloodshed at Islamic shrine.

text.p: Dragging his feet down the narrow alleyway towards al-Aqsa mosque in Jerusalem's Old City, Mohammad Khader said on Friday he felt as if he were going to a battleground rather than to a place of worship.
"I am going to pray," said the 42-year-old Palestinian. "But frankly, I feel scared. This is not an atmosphere for worship. This is an atmosphere for war."

Memories of last week's bloodshed in which Israeli policemen shot dead three Palestinians during stone-throwing clashes at al-Aqsa mosque compound were still fresh in many worshippers' minds as thousands flocked to Friday prayers.
But this week, the prayers ended peacefully under the guns of 3,000 Israeli policemen ringing the Temple Mount, known to Moslems as Haram al-Sharif.
The Islamic fundamentalist Hamas movement had called for "total confrontations" with Israeli forces and settlers after prayers throughout the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
Police randomly stopped young Palestinians for quick interrogations and identity card checks, turning back some worshippers.

For a moment, Islam's third holiest shrine appeared to be on the verge of explosion when about 500 worshippers gathered opposite a contingent of policemen stationed just inside Bab al-Magharbeh, one of the mosques's gates.
Moslem clerics quickly intervened to stop youths from hurling stones at the Israelis.
Tension had been running high since last week when stone- throwing demonstrations and gun battles erupted after Israel opened a new entrance to an archaeological tunnel near the holy site.
Israeli Prime MInister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat failed to resolve differences at a Washington summit this week, raising fears of more violence.

Overcome with worry, a group of veiled women standing on the high courtyard around the seventh-century gold-plated Dome of the Rock mosque pleaded to God to prevent fresh bloodshed as they watched young men running in the al-Aqsa courtyard below.
The women quickly hushed one woman who tried to rush downstairs to incite men to demonstrate.
"Enough bloodshed. Let's not give them (the Israelis) an excuse to do more killings," shouted one Palestinian legislator who attended the prayers.
Palestinian community leaders sighed with relief as worshippers began to disperse. Police snipers on buildings above the compound followed them with their guns.
"Thank God that nothing happened today," said Ahmed al-Batsh, a Palestinian legislator who helped in preventing a new flareup.
